steps.title: Find the place
steps.lead: This is Chokwe, a town in Mozambique. The outlined area covers its main built-up area and the Limpopo River beside it.
body: First NISAR image (5 January 2026); not assumed to be dry or pre-flood. No inspection areas are registered for this event.
Dark areas are low backscatter (smooth surfaces; can be open water); bright areas are high backscatter.
Along the Limpopo, in the north-east of the study area, the low-backscatter river channel is already visible on this date.

Study area: 135.7 km² = the ADM3 unit that contains the town (51.0 km²; not an official city boundary), the built-up area contiguous with it (16.6 km², from OSM buildings, approximate) and the Limpopo surroundings next to the town (68.0 km²). None of these lines is a flood boundary.

steps.title: Spot the change
steps.lead: Blue means the radar signal became weaker. The river side of the area, to the north-east, turned blue.
body: Strong decrease on the river side; increase over the built-up area.

40% of the study area: HH signal down > 3 dB — Share of the whole 135.7 km² study area where the HH radar signal decreased by more than 3 dB (50 m). Not the share of flooded area. The cause of the increase over the built-up area is unknown.

In “Compare radar”, the divider compares the grey images: left 5 January, right 17 January. A northwest–southeast line splits the study area: strong backscatter decrease on the river (north-east) side, increase over the built-up area to the south-west and in the built-up belt to the south-east.

At 50 m scale (10 m grid), the HH radar signal fell by more than 3 dB over 40% of the 135.7 km² study area and rose by more than 3 dB over 18% (denominator: all 1,356,813 pixels, valid on both dates). By part: town unit 38% down / 19% up; contiguous built-up area 2% / 57%; Limpopo surroundings 50% / 7%. These are shares of radar signal change, not shares of flooded area and not a water classification.
Earlier 5 × 5 km trial (centre of the town): 43% down > 3 dB. Recomputed from the new rasters it gives the same value; it describes only that smaller box, not the whole town.
The cause of the increase over the built-up area is unknown; without evidence it is not interpreted as flooding or damage.

Between 5 January and 17 January the HH signal of the whole NISAR image also rose by about 3.0 dB (frame QA statistics); over the town's built-up core it rose by 3.25 dB (median). Much of the increase over the town therefore matches this image-wide level difference between the two BETA images; its cause (calibration or wide-area moisture) is not known.
notes: A drop in backscatter is consistent with open water but is not, on its own, evidence of flooding (wet soil, flooded fields, harvest).
The radar images are 2 separate observations; switching between them is not a real-time view of flood progression.

steps.title: What else do we know?
steps.lead: Clouds covered the area around 17 January, so no normal photo from space could check it. A flood map from another radar satellite (GFM) could check about three quarters of the area.
body: No usable optical image near 17 January.
Copernicus GFM (17 January, 03:18 UTC) was checked over the whole study area as a separate reference (descriptive consistency, not an accuracy measure). It is not shown on this map.

Optical images within 7 days of 17 January: 8 scenes; the best one observed 0% of the study area clearly (provider mask and the experimental haze screen), so independent optical checking was not possible.

Copernicus GFM (Sentinel-1) observed 24 minutes before NISAR (03:18 UTC). In the study area GFM could observe 73% (excluded 27%, no GFM data 0.6%; both GFM tiles of this pass); in the town unit 63%. Where it could observe, it marked flooding in 24% of those places (18% of the whole study area). The three GFM algorithms disagree strongly here (flooded share of the observable area: DLR 3%, LIST 25%, TUW 55%), and GFM's advisory flag is set on 40% of the study area.

Among the pixels with NISAR's strongest decrease (lowest 10% inside the study area; ΔHH below −8.3 dB), GFM marked flooding in 35% of the places it could observe. This was computed with only one of the two GFM tiles of this pass (it could observe 52% of these pixels) and was not recomputed with both.
This is descriptive consistency between two radar products, not an accuracy measure. GFM is not shown as a map layer for this event.

Later maps (UNOSAT 4232: Sentinel-1, 23–24 January; Copernicus EMS EMSR857, image date not verified) were not used as the 17 January boundary. NASA SVS 5661 uses the same NISAR data and is not an independent check.
No water candidate, flood boundary or flood area was produced for this event.
notes: This event is a two-date radar comparison only: no water candidate, flood boundary or flood area was produced.

unknown: Why the radar signal became stronger over the built-up part of the town. The whole radar image was about 3 dB stronger on 17 January, so much of this may not be a local change.
Whether every blue place was flooded.
How big the flooded area was. We did not calculate it.
Many places in the town: GFM could not check them.

HV noise floor: the product's noise layer is given in DN² with an unspecified normalisation. Because it could not be confirmed to be in the same unit as the measured γ⁰, no HV mask was applied. How much low HV values are affected by noise is unknown.
This event is a two-date radar comparison only: no water candidate, flood boundary or flood area was produced.
No usable optical image near 17 January 2026 (scenes around that date are almost fully cloudy over the study area).

Copernicus GFM observed 24 min before NISAR; it is not shown as a layer here and was not used as a flood boundary. GFM could observe 73% of the study area and 63% of the town unit (exclusion mask, mostly built-up; both GFM tiles). Its three algorithms disagree strongly on 17 January (DLR 3%, LIST 25%, TUW 55% flooded of the observable area).

Between 5 January and 17 January the HH signal of the whole NISAR image also rose by about 3.0 dB (frame QA statistics); over the town's built-up core it rose by 3.25 dB (median). Much of the increase over the town therefore matches this image-wide level difference between the two BETA images; its cause (calibration or wide-area moisture) is not known.
The cause of the backscatter increase over the built-up area is unknown; without evidence it must not be interpreted as flooding or damage.
UNOSAT and Copernicus EMS products are based on images after 17 January; they cannot be used as the 17 January boundary.
The products are BETA (CRID X05010): no inputDataExceptionMask, RFI mitigation disabled at L1, partial frame. Validity is from the 'mask' layer only.

The city part of the study area is the ADM3 administrative unit that contains the town (INE/OCHA 2021 via geoBoundaries); it was not checked against the municipal boundary. The contiguous built-up area is approximate (OSM buildings). The Limpopo surroundings are an a-priori 2 km corridor, not a floodplain.
Results apply only to the 135.7 km² study area and cannot be generalised beyond it.
